title: Electric and magnetic fields
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: D.2#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.2#c12 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.2#c13 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.2.8#xt1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D.2#q11, D.2#q14, D.2#q15, D.2#q17, D.2#q12, D.2#q34, D.2#q16, D.2#q18, D.2#q13, D.2#q19, D.2#q20, D.2#q21, D.2#q22, D.2#q23, D.2#q24, D.2#q26.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Electric charge
items.clue: A property of matter of two types, positive and negative; like repel, unlike attract.

items.label: Electrostatic induction
items.clue: A nearby charged object rearranges the free charge in a conductor without touching it.

items.label: Grounding (earthing)
items.clue: Connecting a conductor to a very large reservoir of charge so that it becomes neutral.

items.label: Electric field strength
items.clue: The force per unit charge on a small positive test charge; greater where the pattern is denser.

questions.stem: A student sketches the electric field lines around two equal positive point charges a short distance apart. Which description of a correct sketch is right?

options.text: Lines leave each charge and curve away from the other, with a neutral point at the midpoint.
Lines leave each charge, and some of them cross one another in the region midway between them.
Lines run from one charge to the other, joining the two charges across the gap.
Straight radial lines leave each charge, exactly as if the other charge were absent.

questions.stem: The field lines of an isolated negative point charge spread out in three dimensions, and the same number of lines passes through every sphere centred on the charge. Point P is 2.0 cm from the charge and point Q is 6.0 cm from it. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?

options.text: E at P is 3 times E at Q, as P is 3 times closer, so the lines are 3 times as close.
E is the same at P and Q, as each line that passes P's sphere also passes Q's sphere.
E at P is 9 times E at Q, as there are 9 times as many lines per unit area at P.
E cannot be compared, as the number of field lines drawn is merely an arbitrary choice.

questions.stem: Two parallel metal plates 5.0 mm apart in a vacuum are connected to a 1500 V supply. An electron is between the plates, well away from their edges. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the magnitude of the electric force on the electron?
A long, straight, vertical wire carries a steady current upwards. Point P is 5.0 cm due east of the wire, level with it. What is the direction of the magnetic field of the wire at P?

options.text: Due south, at a tangent to a circle around the wire
Due east, directly away from the wire along a radius
Due north, at a tangent to a circle centred on the wire
Vertically upwards, parallel to the direction of the current

questions.explanation: Right-hand grip rule: thumb upwards along the current, fingers curl anticlockwise when seen from above. The field lines are circles round the wire; at a point east of the wire, anticlockwise means due north.

questions.stem: A hollow metal sphere on an insulating stand is given a positive charge. Which description of the electric field lines is correct?

options.text: Lines inside as well as outside, since the charge is spread through the whole sphere.
None inside; outside, radial lines pointing away, as if from a point charge at the centre.
Lines leave the surface both ways, pointing inwards and outwards from the charge.
None inside; outside, parallel and equally spaced lines, as the charge is spread evenly.

questions.stem: A sketch shows the electric field lines near a charged object. A small positive test charge is placed at a point P that lies midway between two neighbouring field lines, in a region where the lines are closely spaced. Which statement is correct?

options.text: No force acts on it at P, since the electric field exists only along the lines that are drawn.
A force acts on it at P, but its size cannot be judged, as the number of lines drawn is a matter of choice.
A force acts on it at P, of the same size as anywhere between those two lines, as the field is constant along a line.
A force acts on it at P, and the close spacing of the lines shows that the field there is relatively strong.

questions.stem: Two parallel plates remain connected to the same supply while their separation is doubled. A small charged dust particle is held between the plates, well away from their edges. How does the electric force on the particle change?

options.text: It is unchanged, since E depends only on V, which the supply fixes.
It halves, since E = V/d and d has doubled while V is unchanged.
It falls to a quarter, since E ∝ 1/d², like the field of a point charge.
It doubles, since E = Vd and d has doubled at constant V.

questions.explanation: The supply keeps V fixed. Between the plates E = V/d, so doubling d halves E, and F = qE halves.

questions.stem: A flat horizontal circular coil carries a steady current that flows anticlockwise when viewed from above. What is the direction of the magnetic field at the centre of the coil?

options.text: There is no field: the fields of opposite sides cancel out.
Vertically upwards, along the central axis of the coil.
Horizontal, in the plane of the coil, circling like the current.
Vertically downwards, along the central axis of the coil.

questions.explanation: Apply the right-hand grip rule to any part of the coil: with the thumb along the anticlockwise current, the curled fingers pass upwards through the inside of the loop. Every part gives an upward field at the centre, so the field there is vertically upwards, along the axis.

questions.stem: Which description of the electric field lines of two oppositely charged parallel plates is correct?

options.text: Parallel and evenly spaced from the positive to the negative plate, stopping sharply at the plate edges.
From the positive to the negative plate, closest near each plate and widest apart midway.
Closed loops that leave the positive plate and curve round to return to it, as magnetic field lines do.
Parallel and evenly spaced from the positive to the negative plate, bulging outwards at the edges.

questions.explanation: In the central region the field is uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from + to −. Near the edges the lines curve outwards beyond the plates (the edge effect), so the field there is not uniform.

questions.stem: A long air-core solenoid carries a steady current. Which description of its magnetic field lines is correct?

options.text: Almost no field inside; outside, lines loop from one end to the other, as for a bar magnet.
Strongest inside at the two ends, where the lines crowd together, and weakest at the centre.
Lines start at the north-pole end and stop at the south-pole end, so none of them form closed loops.
Parallel, evenly spaced lines inside; outside, like a bar magnet's; each is a closed loop.

questions.explanation: Inside a long solenoid the field is strong and nearly uniform along the axis. Outside, the pattern resembles a bar magnet's. Every line is a closed loop, returning through the inside of the solenoid.

questions.stem: Two small spheres, each carrying a positive charge, are brought from infinite separation to a separation r. Which statement about the electric potential energy E_p of the system is correct?

options.text: It is positive, since positive work must be done to push the like charges together.
It is negative, as it is for two masses, since E_p is zero at infinite separation.
It is stored in the sphere that was moved, not in the system of the two spheres.
It is positive, and it becomes larger if the spheres are moved further apart.

questions.explanation: E_p is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation, where E_p = 0. Like charges repel, so an external force must do positive work to bring them together: E_p = kq₁q₂/r > 0.

questions.stem: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, the electron is 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m from the proton. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹. What is the electric potential energy of the electron–proton system?
questions.explanation: E_p = kq₁q₂/r with k = 1/4πε₀ = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²: E_p = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (+1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)(−1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)/5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ = −4.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (about −27 eV). Negative, because the charges attract.

questions.stem: Four point charges are fixed at the corners of a square of side 0.20 m. Three of the charges are +2.0 nC and the fourth is −2.0 nC. Electric potential is zero at infinity. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the electric potential at the centre of the square?
questions.explanation: Each corner is a/√2 = 0.141 m from the centre. Potential is a scalar: V = kΣq/r = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (2.0 + 2.0 + 2.0 − 2.0) × 10⁻⁹/0.141 = 2.5 × 10² V.

questions.stem: Point P is a distance r from an isolated point charge −Q. Which statement about the electric potential at P is correct?

options.text: It is directed towards the charge, with a size equal to the work done per unit charge from infinity to P.
It is the work done per unit charge to bring a small positive test charge from infinity to P.
It is the potential energy, measured in joules, of any small charge that happens to be placed at P.
It is inversely proportional to r², falling off in the same way as the field strength.

questions.explanation: V_e is defined as the work done per unit charge bringing a small positive test charge from infinity (V = 0) to P. The charge is attracted towards −Q, so this work is negative: V_e = −kQ/r.

questions.stem: In a region of uniform electric field of strength 4.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹ directed in the +x direction, point A at x = 0 has an electric potential of +500 V. What is the electric potential at point B, at x = 0.050 m?
questions.explanation: E = −ΔV/Δx, so ΔV = −EΔx = −(4.0 × 10³)(0.050) = −200 V: potential falls along the field. V_B = 500 V − 200 V = +300 V.

questions.stem: An alpha particle, of charge +2e, is moved at constant speed from a point where the electric potential is +2000 V to a point where it is +500 V. What is the work done on the alpha particle by the external force that moves it?

options.text: +3.0 keV
−3.0 keV
−1.5 keV
+1.0 keV

questions.explanation: W = qΔV_e = (2e)(500 V − 2000 V) = 2e × (−1500 V) = −3000 eV = −3.0 keV (−4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J). The field pushes the positive particle towards lower potential, so the external force must hold it back to keep its speed constant: its work is negative.
